verses.translation_literal: To the leader. A psalm. Of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster: a psalm of David.
verses.directors_commentary: This line is the label on the scroll, and the performers in the Temple are its first audience. The KJV's 'chief Musician' is acceptable for lamnatzeach, though the root natzach means to excel, to preside and to endure, so the title names a leader, not a rank. The 'of David' (ledavid) with the lamed can mean by David, for David or in David's style. Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as David speaking about his illness. The KJV leaves this line as verse 0, which is why every number in this chapter is one ahead of the English Bible.

philological_notes.note: The participle 'one who leads, presides', from a root that also means 'to be eminent' or 'to last'. It is the director's title in the Psalter's superscriptions. The meaning of the title is debated and I gave its traditional sense, 'to the leader'.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [is] the one who considers the weak one; in a day of evil YHWH will deliver him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Happy is the one who stops and thinks of the weak, who sees them and does not look away. When the evil day comes for such a person, the LORD himself will pull them out of it.
verses.directors_commentary: Open on a note of calm, the voice of a teacher quoting a proverb. 'Blessed' (ashrei) is not a feeling but a status: the road is straight for this person. The verb maskil means to act with insight, not only to 'consider'. The KJV's 'considereth' is too passive, since the Hebrew person thinks and then does something. The Hebrew dal means thin, slack and weak. It covers the poor, and it is also the word Jonadab uses for the sick Amnon in 2 Samuel 13:4 ('why are you so thin, king's son?'). Rashi and Radak therefore hear a sick person here, and the visitor at the bedside who is blessed. Malbim and Metzudat David hear the poor. Both readings fit, and the psalm's sickbed supports the first. 'The day of evil' (yom ra'ah) is the day of disaster, which Rashi reads as Gehenna, Radak as the day the illness grows heavy. Note the KJV's 'time of trouble' is softer than the Hebrew 'evil'. The last word is YHWH, held to the end of the sentence, so the rescuer arrives as the final beat.

philological_notes.note: To act with insight and success. Not mere thinking: the one who 'considers' does something. Ibn Ezra relates it to 'looking at', then prefers a derivation from sechel, mind.
Lean, low, weak. It names material poverty and bodily weakness together. Rashi and Radak quote 2 Samuel 13:4 for 'sick'.

token_glosses.gloss: the one who considers (acts with insight)

verses.translation_literal: YHWH will guard him and keep him alive, and he will be called blessed in the land, and do not give him over to the desire of his enemies.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD will watch over such a one and keep the breath in them. They will be called happy across the land. And you, LORD, will never hand them over to what their enemies want.
verses.directors_commentary: Four promises follow one another in a rush: guard, keep alive, bless, shield. Then the sentence turns to speak to God directly in 'do not give him' (ve'al titteNehu). The KJV smooths that into 'thou wilt not deliver', but the Hebrew has the particle al, which is normally a plea ('do not'), so the line wavers between promise and prayer. Radak and Ibn Ezra both notice this. Play it as a statement of trust that is half a prayer. The written text (Ketiv) has 'he will be called blessed' with a yod, the Qere with a waw. The meaning is the same. 'Desire' translates nefesh, which is literally throat or appetite, the hunger of the enemies. The KJV's 'will' is a pale rendering of a word with teeth in it, and Radak glosses it as the enemies' wish that he should die.

philological_notes.note: Nefesh here means appetite or wish (literally the throat that gulps). Metzudat Zion compares Genesis 23:8, 'if it is your nefesh'. So the enemies have a hunger, and the line says: do not hand him to it.

token_glosses.gloss: and he will keep him alive
and he will be called blessed (Qere)

verses.translation_literal: YHWH will sustain him upon a couch of sickness; all his lying-place you have turned in his illness.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD will hold up such a one, even there, on the couch where sickness has laid them down. And you, LORD, have seen how the bed itself was undone, the place made for rest turned into a place of pain, all of it, through the long hours of the illness.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse changes voice in the middle: 'YHWH will sustain him' is spoken about the sick person, and 'you have turned' is spoken to God. Play the second half as a quiet turn toward heaven, not a change of subject. Rashi, in the commentary he takes from the Aggadah on Psalms, ties 'couch of sickness' to the seventh day of an illness, when it is at its worst.

The verb hafakh is 'turn, overturn', and the line is hard. Radak's first reading is that the bed, which a healthy person takes as a place of rest, has been turned by God from rest into suffering (Meiri reads it the same way), and 'all' (kol) is there because the sick lie in it day and night. The other reading is a nurse's: Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David take the turning as God turning the patient from one side to the other, as an attendant would, because the patient has no one to do it. Radak also offers a prayer reading, with hafakhta as 'turn!': turn all his bed in his sickness to health and rest. The KJV's 'thou wilt make all his bed' follows none of these, since the Hebrew has no verb for making a bed. It also softens sa'ad, 'support, prop up', into 'strengthen', and 'bed of languishing' for 'eres dvay, a couch of sickness, is Elizabethan and vague. An 'eres is a real piece of furniture, a frame; Deuteronomy 3:11 uses it for Og's iron bedstead, and the sick would lie on one at home, with family close and few remedies.

philological_notes.note: To support, prop up, sustain, as a person is held up by a hand or a pillow; the noun sa'ad is 'support'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as support (smikhah). The KJV 'strengthen' makes it about vigor; the Hebrew is about being held while weak.

Perfect, 'you have turned'. Radak reads the bed as turned from rest into trouble (Meiri agrees); Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read a turning of the body from side to side; Radak's alternative reads it as a prayer, 'turn!'.

verses.translation_literal: I, I said: YHWH, show me favor; heal my life, for I have sinned against you.
verses.translation_dramatic: As for me, I said it aloud: LORD, be gracious to me. Heal me, heal the very life in me, for I have sinned against you.
verses.directors_commentary: The proverb ends and a man speaks. 'I, I said' puts the weight on the pronoun: after the blessed visitor, here is the sufferer, and he is the one who speaks. In the KJV 'I said' is flat, but the Hebrew ani amarti leans on ani as a contrast with 'they' who are about to appear. His prayer is for mercy, then for healing of the nefesh. The KJV renders it 'soul', which is a Greek-flavoured word. Nefesh is the whole living self, throat and breath included, so 'heal my life' is also 'heal my body'. Radak notes that the man did not say 'heal my body', because he thinks the illness comes from sin, and that forgiveness will heal the body. BBE's 'my faith is in you' mistranslates the end of the line, which is plain confession: 'I have sinned against you'. In the ancient world, serious illness was understood as divine judgment, and so this is not a pious flourish, it is a diagnosis.

philological_notes.note: 'Heal my self.' Nefesh is the whole living person, so the prayer covers body and spirit. Radak argues that forgiveness is the cure of the nefesh and bodily healing follows.

verses.translation_literal: My enemies say evil for me: when will he die, and his name perish?
verses.translation_dramatic: My enemies speak, and what they say is dark. 'When will he die?' they ask. 'When will his name be gone?'
verses.directors_commentary: The mood changes from prayer to menace. Enemies stand around the sickroom, and what they ask is not rhetorical; it is a wish that sounds like a question. In the ancient world a name was a person's afterlife: the family line, the property, the memory. To wish 'his name perish' (ve'avad shemo) is to wish for him to be erased, not only to die. The KJV, 'Mine enemies speak evil of me', is adequate but misses the unspoken sting of the Hebrew ra' li, 'evil for me', in which the evil is spoken in order to bring it about. Ibn Ezra and Radak hear the enemies contradicting the blessing of verse 2. Sound: the two short verbs, yamut and ve'avad, fall like a gavel.

philological_notes.note: 'His name perishes.' The name is the person's continuing presence: descendants, memory, standing. The wish is for total extinction.

verses.translation_literal: And if he has come to see [me], falsehood he speaks; his heart gathers iniquity for itself; he goes out to the outside, he speaks.
verses.translation_dramatic: And if one of them comes to see me, what a performance of words, and not one of them true. All the while the heart is at work, gathering up every ugly thing to keep for itself. Then he is gone, out the door, out into the street, and there at last he speaks.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene is a sickroom visit, and the visitor is a hypocrite. The verb 'speak' comes twice (yedaber ... yedaber), at the opening and at the close, and the sound matters: in the room he speaks falsehood (shav'), in the street he speaks what he has stored. In the middle the heart does its own work: libbo is the subject of yikbotz, 'it gathers'. The heart is the seat of thought, and here it collects. Rashi has the visitor look as if he were grieved while his heart gathers evil thoughts to say once outside.

The commentators fill in what is said in the room differently. Radak gives it as words of comfort with no good in the heart, and also the version of his father, who read the visitor as mixing soft and hard words to break the patient's heart; Ibn Ezra's example is 'how it angers me that you are sick'. The KJV 'he speaketh vanity' is sound, and 'when he goeth abroad, he telleth it' makes the Hebrew's two bare verbs easier. Hebrew gives only 'he goes out to the outside, he speaks', with the consequence left hanging, and you should leave it hanging. 'Gathereth iniquity' keeps 'aven, which is trouble and wickedness together. In a village an illness was public property, and the visit was a duty; this man pays the call and then trades what he saw.

philological_notes.note: Emptiness, falsehood, what has nothing in it. Here it is words of sympathy that are hollow. The KJV 'vanity' keeps the sense of empty but loses the charge of lying.

'It gathers', with libbo ('his heart') as the subject: the heart is the seat of thought, and it collects. Rashi: his heart gathers thoughts of wickedness for himself, what ill to say once out. Radak: it is gathered in the heart and not let out until he is outside.

verses.translation_literal: Together against me they whisper, all who hate me; against me they devise evil for me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then they huddle. All who hate me draw close and murmur about me, heads together, and in the murmur they plot my harm.
verses.directors_commentary: The camera moves from the visitor to the gathering of haters. The verb yitlachashu comes from lachash, a hiss or murmur, the sound of a whisper that carries no words to the one it is about. Hear it: the sibilants (yitlachashu, kol sone'ai) fill the line with hissing. The KJV's 'whisper together' is right, but then 'my hurt' makes it sound like an injury already done, when the Hebrew says they plan ra'ah li, 'evil for me'. Note the repeated 'against me' (alai ... alai): the whole world in this line has turned to face one man. Radak sees the visitor of verse 7 joining the rest.

philological_notes.note: A reflexive stem, 'they whisper to one another'. Lachash is also the word for a charm or incantation, so the whispers may carry a hint of magic spoken at the sick man.

verses.translation_literal: A thing of worthlessness is poured out on him; and where he lay down, he will not again rise.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'Something foul has been poured into him,' they say. 'He lay down, and he will not get up again.'
verses.directors_commentary: These are the whispers themselves, in direct speech, though the Hebrew gives no 'say they'; the KJV inserts it and also 'an evil disease', which settles a question the Hebrew leaves open. Devar-beliya'al is literally 'a thing of beliya'al', a word that means worthlessness, wickedness, and later a name for the devil. It could be a curse, a crime or an illness. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as his own sin, which has been poured into his body, like molten metal. Radak reads it as a grave disease clinging to him, with a comparison to Job 41:16, where a heart is 'cast' hard as stone. Malbim goes further and reads poison. The verb yatzuq is the one for casting metal or pouring oil, so the image is of a substance cooling into something that sticks. The second half is cruel in its simplicity: 'he lay down; he will not add to rise'. Play it as a verdict said with satisfaction.

philological_notes.note: A 'thing of worthlessness'. It may be a curse, a crime or a disease, and the commentators divide on this. Metzudat Zion derives beliya'al as 'without the yoke of heaven' (beli ol).
Poured, cast, as of molten metal that sets hard. Radak compares Job 41:16 for 'sticks fast'.

verses.translation_literal: Even the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, the eater of my bread, has made great against me a heel.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even the man I was at peace with, the one I trusted, the one who ate my bread, has made his heel big against me.
verses.directors_commentary: The pain is personal now. 'The man of my peace' (ish shelomi) is more than a friend: he is the one who greeted with shalom, a covenant ally. Eating another's bread was the strongest bond of hospitality in the ancient Near East, because shared food sealed protection; to betray the host was to break the oldest rule there was. The KJV's 'lifted up his heel' is the well-known version, but the Hebrew says higdil alai akev, 'made the heel great against me'. The meaning is uncertain: it may be kicking or trampling, as Radak thinks ('he makes himself big over me, as if treading me'), or ambush, as Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat David read it, from akev in Joshua 8:13, 'the rear of the city'. Ibn Ezra offers a third reading: he exaggerated his heel, he did not come to visit. The word also brings up Jacob, the heel-grabber, whose name comes from the same root, and so the sound of betrayal is Jacob's. The translation 'lifted up' is a softening and a guess.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'made the heel great against me'. A trampling, a kick, or an ambush, since akev can mean 'rear guard'. Rashi and Metzudat David choose ambush with Joshua 8:13; Radak chooses trampling.
'The man of my peace': a close ally, one with whom one exchanged shalom as a pledge.

verses.translation_literal: And you, YHWH, show me favor and raise me up, and let me repay them.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you, LORD. You. Be gracious to me and lift me from this bed, and let me pay them back.
verses.directors_commentary:
'And you' is the hinge of the psalm: after the whisperers and the friend with the heel, the speaker turns to the only one who can answer. 'Raise me up' (haqimeni) is the exact reply to verse 9, where the whisperers say 'he will not rise again' (lo yosif laqum). Ibn Ezra notes that haqimeni answers 'lo yosif laqum' and chonneni answers 'devar beliyya'al yatzuq bo'. Say it as an answer to what they said, and not as a general plea.

The last word is the difficulty. va'ashallemah is a cohortative of shillem, 'repay, pay in full', with 'let me' in it. The KJV 'that I may requite them' and the BBE 'give them their punishment' take it as revenge. Radak does not: he says the Psalmist does not mean harm to them, and cites Psalm 7:5, and he reads the repayment as withholding sympathy. When they fall ill, I will not wear sackcloth, will not pray for them, will not grieve at their troubles. He also reports from the Gaon, Rabbenu Saadia, as cited by him, the opposite turn: repaying them good in place of evil, as in Psalm 35:13, 'and I, in their sickness, my clothing was sackcloth'. Meiri has the Psalmist as the cause of their punishment, and Metzudat David 'as they deserve'. Whichever you choose as the director, play the line with the face of someone who has been wronged and has not yet decided what to do with the power he asks for.

philological_notes.note: Cohortative of the piel of shalem, 'let me repay, make whole the account'. It can mean requital, punishment, or paying back in kind. Radak: the repayment is that he will not wear sackcloth in their illness or pray for them; he also gives Saadia Gaon (as cited by Radak) for repaying good for evil, as in Psalm 35:13. Meiri reads the Psalmist as the cause of their punishment, Metzudat David 'as they deserve'.
Hiphil imperative, 'raise me up', the answer to 'he will not rise again' (laqum) in verse 9.

verses.translation_literal: By this I know that you delight in me, that my enemy does not shout in triumph over me.
verses.translation_dramatic: By this I will know that you take pleasure in me: my enemy does not raise his victory shout over me.
verses.directors_commentary: Here is the test of favor, and it is public. The verb yari'a is the teru'ah, the great shout of the winning army, of a crowd at a coronation or of a horn at a feast. It is the opposite of the whisper in the corners. The enemy's cheer is what the sick man dreads most, and silence from that side is his proof of divine love. The KJV's 'favourest me' is soft for chafatzta bi, 'you take delight in me', which has the warmth of a father's pleasure. Radak and Rashi read the verb as future or conditional: when God raises him, then he will know. The tenses are open, and I kept the present in the literal line for the Hebrew perfect 'I know' and made the drama a promise. The verse closes the first movement of the psalm, and the ending comes down on 'over me', alai, the word that the enemies have used all through the verses before.

philological_notes.note: To raise the teru'ah, the shout of war or joy. Metzudat David defines it as a shout of joy; Ibn Ezra compares it to the victor's shout in battle, from Psalm 60:10.
'You take delight in me.' It is stronger than 'favor': a wish and a pleasure together.

verses.translation_literal: And I, in my integrity you have held me, and you have set me before your face for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I, I who was on that bed, am held. You took hold of me in my wholeness, and you have stood me upright before your face, to stay there, always.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the long fall into enemies and sickness, the voice rests: 'And I' answers the 'they' of the preceding verses. Notice the sound: tummi tamakhta, 'in my integrity you have held', two words that rhyme on t-m. The grip of tamakh is God's hand under a falling person, and it is the same act as sa'ad in verse 4.

The KJV 'thou upholdest me in mine integrity' reads tummi as moral integrity, as does Ibn Ezra first ('because of my integrity'), and Metzudat David ('because I walked in wholeness'). But Ibn Ezra then prefers another reading: tummi alludes to the soundness of the body, and he calls this the right one. That fits a sickbed, where 'whole' means 'well', and I would let it color the line: you held me in my wholeness, in the health that is given back to me. Radak keeps both senses together (found pure and upright; healthy and sound). 'Set me before your face for ever' (le'olam) is, for Radak, 'for the span of a human life', that I not die before my time; for Meiri it points to eternal life. Radak adds that the Hebrew puts past tense where the sense is future, as is the custom.

philological_notes.note: 'In my wholeness, soundness, integrity'. Ibn Ezra first gives 'because of my integrity', then prefers the view that tummi refers to the soundness of the body. Radak reads it as 'found pure and upright'.
To grasp, take hold of and keep up. It echoes tummi in sound.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [is] YHWH, God of Israel, from the age and until the age. Amen and amen.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed is the LORD, the God of Israel, from the age before ages to the age that has no end. So it is. So it is.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse is not the story of the psalm but the closing of a book. It ends Book One of the Psalter (Psalms 1 to 41), and Radak says the Psalmist gives thanks at the end of each of the first four books, as is the scribes' custom. Ibn Ezra and Meiri also read it as the close of the first book. Do not play it as a new scene: the sick man is well, and the voice turns outward from private rescue to a doxology the whole congregation can say.

The Hebrew baruch is a passive participle with no verb: 'Blessed YHWH'. The KJV's 'Blessed be' reads it as a wish, and the YLT's 'Blessed is' as a declaration; the Hebrew leaves both open, and the literal layer takes 'is'. 'From the age and until the age' (min ha'olam ve'ad ha'olam) is the Hebrew idiom for all time, and the KJV's 'from everlasting, and to everlasting' is fine. The Hebrew keeps the same word for both ends. The double 'amen' (aman, 'firm') is not 'so be it' twice: Radak says it is the confirmation of the blessing, as when a person answers amen after a blessing to confirm it, and Metzudat Zion says the doubling strengthens it. The Targum has the righteous say it.

philological_notes.note: A passive participle, 'blessed', with no verb of being; Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'praised'. Whether it is wish or statement is left open.
From the root of firmness and reliability. Radak: qiyyum, 'confirmation', as one answers amen after a blessing; the doubling strengthens it, as Metzudat Zion says.
